section_summary: This section covers extensive economic, administrative, and spiritual mobilization measures undertaken in Japan under the National General Mobilization Law during late 1938, as detailed in an Embassy memorandum by Max W. Schmidt and despatches by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. It describes the government's import-export 'link' system, commodity price regulations, unemployment and labor transfer policies, spiritual mobilization campaigns, and the reorganization of wartime administrative boards to prepare for a single national party structure. The concluding documents track the January 1939 political crisis marked by the resignation of Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe's Cabinet and the installation of a more authoritarian ministry under Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma.

subfiles.about: Detailed report on Japan's wartime economic controls, labor redistribution, spiritual mobilization, and emerging administrative structures under the National General Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of Third Secretary Max W. Schmidt's memorandum analyzes the reorganization of Japan's domestic economy, including the import-export link system, anti-profiteering measures, and capital mobilization through public savings. It addresses technical unemployment resulting from material rationing and outlines government plans to retrain and redirect labor into war industries or emigration. The report also details spiritual mobilization efforts, newly established administrative organs across ministries, Diet debates over executive decree powers, and the political trajectory toward a single national party. Two appendices provide a contemporary press account of pending mobilization ordinances and an excerpted 1936 Army pamphlet on national mobilization doctrine.
subfiles.title: Mobilization in Japan

subfiles.about: Acknowledgment by the Department of State of Ambassador Grew's despatch No. 3380 enclosing Max W. Schmidt's memorandum on Japanese mobilization.
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State George S. Messersmith acknowledges receipt of Tokyo despatch No. 3380 of November 1, 1938, which transmitted the memorandum 'Mobilization in Japan' prepared by Third Secretary Max W. Schmidt. Messersmith instructs Ambassador Grew to inform Schmidt that the Department found his carefully prepared memorandum of timely interest and usefulness.
subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Despatch No. 3380 on National Mobilization

subfiles.about: State Department cross-reference sheet regarding a memorandum by Hamilton on the Far Eastern situation and potential Japanese peace terms.
subfiles.summary: A cross-reference note directing readers to decimal file 793.94/14403 for a memorandum dated November 11, 1938, by Maxwell M. Hamilton of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. The underlying memorandum reviews background events and complications of the Sino-Japanese conflict and outlines likely Japanese settlement terms according to Japanese observer Yusuke Tsurumi.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Far Eastern situation (Sino-Japanese conflict)

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 3505 on Japanese spiritual mobilization.
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury summarizes Tokyo despatch No. 3505 for Political Adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck, detailing the Japanese Cabinet's announcement of a comprehensive national organization intended to revive the ineffective Central League for Spiritual Mobilization. The memorandum notes adverse press reactions citing unconstitutionality and bureaucratic instability. It highlights the Embassy's assessment that Premier Konoe intends the body to politically integrate the public prior to establishing a single national party on fascist lines.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3505: Government Attempt at National Spiritual Mobilization

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting the Japanese Cabinet's plans to create a nationwide organization (National Council) to reorganize spiritual mobilization and prepare for a single national party.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that efforts toward domestic solidarity culminated in Cabinet plans for a comprehensive National Council (Kokumin Kyogikai) absorbing the Central League for Spiritual Mobilization. Existing political parties offered conditional cooperation while defending their prerogatives, and the domestic press voiced skepticism over constitutional limits and Home Ministry dominance. Grew observes that while Premier Konoe views Japan as not yet ready for a formal totalitarian party along European lines, the new council is designed to achieve preparatory political regimentation. An enclosed clipping from The Japan Advertiser outlines the proposed administrative structure and Cabinet deliberations.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3505: Government Attempt at National Spiritual Mobilization

subfiles.about: Telegraphic report from Tokyo relaying rumors of impending Cabinet reorganization, peace talks with Wang Ching-wei, or the resignation of Premier Konoe.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports heightened political activity in Tokyo and circulating rumors that Premier Konoe may resign in favor of General Minami, Baron Hiranuma, or Marquis Kido, that the Cabinet may be streamlined, or that peace proposals are being framed with Wang Ching-wei. Due to the New Year holidays, reliable verification is limited, but Embassy contacts suggest Konoe cannot resign responsibly at this juncture. Grew assesses the rumors of resignation and peace talks as exaggerated explanations for a more probable, routine Cabinet reorganization.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 813 from Tokyo Regarding Political Rumors and Possible Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Confidential State Department paraphrase of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 813 regarding Japanese political tension and resignation rumors.
subfiles.summary: A confidential paraphrase prepared by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizing Tokyo Telegram No. 813. It recaps current Tokyo rumors concerning Cabinet reconstruction, potential prime ministerial successors (Minami, Hiranuma, Kido), and peace negotiations with Wang Ching-wei. The text notes the Embassy's skepticism regarding Konoe's immediate resignation and its view that Cabinet reorganization represents the only probable core of the rumors.
subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 813 of December 29, 1938, from Tokyo

subfiles.about: Telegraphic instruction requesting confirmation of press reports regarding the establishment of the China Affairs Board.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of State Sumner Welles instructs the American Embassy in Tokyo to telegraph whether press reports announcing the establishment of the China Affairs Board are accurate. If the board has been established, the Embassy is directed to submit a comprehensive report by mail.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 435 to Tokyo Regarding China Affairs Board

subfiles.about: Telegraphic confirmation from Tokyo that the China Affairs Board was formally organized and operational.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew replies to the Department's inquiry, confirming that organic regulations for the China Affairs Board were promulgated on December 16, 1938, on which date the board was formally organized and began functioning. He adds that a comprehensive report was forwarded in Embassy despatch No. 3549 on December 23.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 818 from Tokyo Reporting on China Affairs Board

subfiles.about: Urgent telegram announcing the resignation of the Konoe Cabinet on January 4, 1939.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits an urgent telegraphic flash reporting that the entire Japanese Cabinet headed by Prince Fumimaro Konoe resigned on the morning of January 4, 1939.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 4 from Tokyo Announcing Resignation of Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegraphic report on prospective ministerial appointments and political maneuvering following the Konoe Cabinet's resignation.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports press forecasts indicating War Minister Itagaki, Justice Minister Shiono, and Welfare Minister Kido will remain in the government, while Home Minister Suetsugu, Finance Minister Ikeda, and other ministers will depart. Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma is anticipated as the next Premier, with Prince Konoe slated to replace him as President of the Privy Council. Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Yuasa is reported traveling to Prince Saionji to secure elder statesman approval for Hiranuma's appointment.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 5 from Tokyo on Successor Cabinet Prospects

subfiles.about: Biographical memorandum summarizing the career, political record, and chauvinist affiliations of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury reviews the political career of 71-year-old Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma upon his nomination as Prime Minister. The memorandum outlines his judicial background, his role as founder and leader of patriotic reactionary societies, and his popularity among military chauvinists contrasted with strong moderate distrust. It recalls that insurgent officers in the February 26, 1936 incident demanded Hiranuma's premiership.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma

subfiles.about: Telegraphic assessment of Prince Konoe's public resignation statement and the authoritarian implications of Hiranuma's succession.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew analyzes Premier Konoe's ambiguous midday resignation announcement, wherein Konoe claimed that with the conclusion of major military hostilities and the onset of the political reconstruction stage in Japan and China, a fresh government would revitalize public confidence. Grew assesses that Hiranuma's virtually certain accession demonstrates that Konoe was unable to halt the growing domestic tide toward authoritarian governance.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 6 from Tokyo on Motives Behind Konoe's Resignation

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing the domestic economic and military pressures precipitating the Konoe Cabinet crisis.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine examines the underlying causes of the Konoe Cabinet's fall, pointing to Konoe's unfulfilled Diet pledge not to invoke mobilization measures during the China incident. He notes that persistent military demands for harsher domestic economic controls placed Konoe and Finance Minister Ikeda in an unsustainable bind. Ballantine concludes that the crisis stemmed from domestic economic disputes rather than foreign policy disagreements and signifies consolidated Army control over the government.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Significance of the Cabinet Crisis in Japan

subfiles.about: Telegraphic notice of Baron Hiranuma's installation as Prime Minister and the composition of the new inner Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports radio confirmation that Baron Hiranuma has been installed as Prime Minister, with Prince Konoe assuming the presidency of the Privy Council and joining the Cabinet as Minister without portfolio. Members of the former inner Cabinet—Arita, Itagaki, Yonai, and Konoe—remain in the ministry, while Finance Minister Ikeda has departed.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 9 from Tokyo Announcing Installation of Hiranuma Cabinet

subfiles.about: Detailed telegraphic report on the complete ministerial lineup, party representation, and inaugural statement of the Hiranuma Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the full ministerial roster of the Hiranuma Cabinet, noting concurrent postings for Hatta and Shiono, Marquis Kido's appointment to Home Affairs, and the promotion of bureaucratic vice-ministers Ishiwata and Hirose alongside party representatives Maeda (Seiyukai) and Sakurauchi (Minseito). The Cabinet's inaugural statement reiterated national unity and adherence to established China policy. Grew reports that while official circles deny any policy clash triggered the change, some foreign observers speculate that tensions over military policy toward the Soviet Union played a role.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 14 from Tokyo on Hiranuma Cabinet Personnel and Policies
